card.hook: Picture a giant copper-roofed castle perched on a cliff, with you trying to fit all of it in your phone without a stranger's elbow in the corner. That's the Château Frontenac, and it's an easy one to love.
card.stand_here: Stand on Terrasse Dufferin, the boardwalk directly in front of the hotel near the Dufferin kiosk. Face north-west towards the hotel, with the St. Lawrence River behind you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole façade and roof in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the towers, turrets and copper roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line a tower up with a vertical line, and keep your phone level instead of tilting it up, so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early, before the tour buses arrive. One local guide gives about 6:30 AM in summer and 8:30 AM in winter. The terrace gets very crowded in summer and during cruise season.
card.selfie_here: For a quiet selfie, try the far south-west corner of Parc Montmorency, just past the Cartier monument at the corner of rue Port-Dauphine and Côte de la Montagne. Guides say you get a clear view of the hotel with no other people in the frame. Or walk mid-way along the Dufferin Terrace boardwalk early (around 7 to 8 a.m.), face the river and use the front camera with the hotel over your shoulder. Zoom 0.5x helps fit more of the building in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner of rue Notre-Dame and rue du Cul-de-Sac and shoot up the lane, while you stand in the lane below the hotel so the whole building towers behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Terrasse Dufferin is a free, open public boardwalk. It runs along the cliff edge, so watch your footing while you back up for the shot.
card.challenge: Find a tower, line it up with a gridline so it stands up straight, and see if you can get the shot with zero strangers in it.
card.good_to_know: The Château Frontenac was designed by New York architect Bruce Price for the Canadian Pacific Railway and opened in 1893. It has 18 floors, stands about 80 metres tall, and was inspired by medieval châteaux in France's Loire Valley. It became a National Historic Site of Canada in 1981, and an earlier building, the Château Haldimand, stood here until it was demolished in 1892.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Terrasse Dufferin, the boardwalk directly in front of the hotel near the Dufferin kiosk. Face north-west towards the hotel, with the St. Lawrence River behind you.

card.hook: Here's one for the group chat: these falls are about 30 m higher than Niagara. Picture a tall white ribbon of water against a dark cliff, and you've got your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on La Baronne, the clifftop observation deck beside the falls. The falls are close by, to the north-east, so face that way and you'll look at the cascade from a tighter, closer angle than from the bridge.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole scene. Then try 2x-5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the cascade, and 0.5x when you want the gorge and Île d'Orléans in the same shot.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white water, then slide it a little darker so the foam keeps its detail instead of turning plain white.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. It's the calmest time, and one photo guide says it's before the crowds arrive. In summer the water can look a bit yellowish from the iron in the riverbed, which gives the scene a warmer colour.
card.selfie_here: Try the small La Baronne deck, which frames the cascade tightly so the falls can sit behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold your arm up so the water is over your shoulder. The footbridge at the base of the falls is another easy option, a short walk rather than a climb.
card.ask_someone: For a wider shot of you with the falls, ask someone on the Manoir Montmorency terrace, behind the Manoir at the top of the park, to take it.
card.rules_and_safety: At the base of the 487-step staircase the ground is often slippery, so keep your footing steady. The park charges admission, and the staircase can be closed in winter or for repairs, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo each from La Baronne, the suspension bridge and the Escalier Panoramique, then see which angle wins.
card.good_to_know: The falls drop 83 m into the St Lawrence River, at the mouth of the Montmorency River, about 12 km from the heart of old Quebec City. The park has staircases, a suspension bridge and a funitel, so allow time to walk between viewpoints. The bridge looks down the drop toward the river and the skyline, while the Escalier Panoramique looks up through the spray.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on La Baronne, the clifftop observation deck beside the falls. The falls are close by, to the north-east, so face that way and you'll look at the cascade from a tighter, closer angle than from the bridge.

card.hook: Here's a fun fact to warm you up: the battle that decided Quebec City's fate was over in about half an hour, but this park is so big you could easily spend longer just finding the right spot for your photo. Good news, we've found it.
card.stand_here: Head onto the Plains and stand on Pierre-Dugua-De Mons Terrace. Face across the lawn and the St. Lawrence River toward the Château Frontenac and the old city skyline.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the lawns, the river and the skyline into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Château Frontenac and the rooftops in the distance.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper line if you love the sky, or the lower line if the river is the star, with some grass or a path edge in the foreground.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light. Check the weather first, because a clear day shows off the river and the distant skyline best.
card.selfie_here: The terrace itself is a good selfie spot, and visitors say photos here look postcard-worthy in any season. Use the front camera at 0.5x and try to get the view over your shoulder, then check the frame before you move on, as it's not confirmed which way gives the best backdrop. The Remains of the Blockhouse is another option, with the river and city in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is public, but the museum, tours and events may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the whole view in it, then one close shot of just the Château Frontenac, and see which one your friends like more.
card.good_to_know: British and French forces fought here on 13 September 1759, and the battle left Quebec City in British hands. The park was created on 17 March 1908 and became the first National Historic Site in Canada. It covers about 98 hectares, is roughly 2.4 km long, and around four million people visit each year, so wear comfortable shoes.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head onto the Plains and stand on Pierre-Dugua-De Mons Terrace. Face across the lawn and the St. Lawrence River toward the Château Frontenac and the old city skyline.

card.hook: Picture a tiny cobbled square where a church front, a bust of a French king and a ring of steep-roofed stone houses all squeeze into one photo. That's Place Royale, and yes, it really does look like that.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Royale at the eastern end of the square, facing the church front of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires. The middle of the square is to the south of you, about 1 minute on foot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the church, the cobbles and the houses together. Switch to 1x for a more natural look at the church front, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the church door, the bust or the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, keep the church front centred with the cobbles filling the bottom of the shot, and tap the church front, then drag the brightness slider darker if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 9 AM, when the square is at its quietest and most atmospheric. Late afternoon can bring warmer light onto the house fronts, and if the square is busy, rue Dalhousie may give you a quieter, closer-in angle (check it on the map first).
card.selfie_here: Stand in the square in front of the stone facade of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires with the church behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it on the front so more of the church and square fits in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at a corner of the square and shoot diagonally across, so the roofs and church tower fill the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Wear comfortable, non-slip shoes, because the old streets are narrow, hilly and paved with uneven cobblestones. Businesses or events can occupy parts of the square and block some of the view, so check beforehand if you need it clear.
card.challenge: Can you get the church front, the Louis XIV bust and at least two stone houses into one shot without anyone walking through it? Take a few in a row and see who wins.
card.good_to_know: Samuel de Champlain founded the settlement here in 1608, which is why the square is often called the cradle of French civilization in America. The stone houses went up after a fire in 1682 destroyed the earlier wooden buildings. The bust of Louis XIV is a replica of the 1686 original and gives the square its name.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place Royale at the eastern end of the square, facing the church front of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires. The middle of the square is to the south of you, about 1 minute on foot.

card.hook: Here's a church that has been burned down and rebuilt more than once, and it still looks calm and tidy in a phone photo. The pale stone front, the tower and the symmetry do half the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville, the square in front of the cathedral in Old Québec, and face the church. You should see the Seminary of Quebec peeking out behind it on the left, with older buildings around the edges.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit the whole front, the square and the buildings around it. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Go to 2x or 5x, depending on your phone, for the tower and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the church up with the vertical lines, and keep your phone level and upright so the walls don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Go early for the quietest square. In the evening there can be live music and street performers, which is lively but puts more people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville with the cathedral's main front behind you, use the front camera and keep the church over your shoulder. For a quieter backdrop, try the Pilgrims' Garden on the north side, near the Holy Door, where the building stays in the frame. If your front camera has 0.5x, it helps fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the square far enough back to take in the whole front, while you stand with the cathedral behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cathedral is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements. No selfie sticks are allowed inside, flash is a no, and please don't photograph during Mass or private prayer.
card.challenge: Take three frames of the front from different distances, then pick the one where the walls stand straight and the tower looks proudest.
card.good_to_know: A chapel built by Samuel de Champlain stood on this spot in 1633, and the church is often described as the oldest in Canada. It became a minor basilica in 1874 and is now a National Historic Site of Canada. It was rebuilt after fires in 1759 and 1922, and the present front dates from a reconstruction proposed in 1843.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville, the square in front of the cathedral in Old Québec, and face the church. You should see the Seminary of Quebec peeking out behind it on the left, with older buildings around the edges.

card.hook: Picture a long wooden boardwalk running straight at a grand hotel, with a wide river on the other side. From up high, Dufferin Terrace looks like it was laid out just for your phone.
card.stand_here: Head up to Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons Terrace, the elevated lookout above the boardwalk, with Dufferin Terrace to the north of you. Face the boardwalk so the Château Frontenac and the St. Lawrence River sit beyond it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the boardwalk, the hotel and the river in one shot. If it's busy, or you want the whole length of the boardwalk, tap 0.5x. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the gazebos and the hotel towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the boardwalk up with a grid line so it leads your eye to the hotel, then tap the hotel and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon is usually calmer and kinder to the light than midday. In cruise season and summer, street performers and crowds fill the boardwalk, so wait for people to wander out of your frame.
card.selfie_here: Take it right here on Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons Terrace, where the raised lookout puts the boardwalk in the background. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze more in, and keep the view over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Parts of the terrace can be steep, cobbled or gravelly, and the walkway under the terrace isn't always open, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: There are six named gazebos along the boardwalk, so see how many repeating little shapes you can fit into one wide shot.
card.good_to_know: The terrace was built under the Marquess of Dufferin, then Governor General of Canada, and opened on 28 June 1879. Parks Canada looks after it. At the southern end, a 150-metre ramp turns into a toboggan run during the Quebec Winter Carnival.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons Terrace, the elevated lookout above the boardwalk, with Dufferin Terrace to the north of you. Face the boardwalk so the Château Frontenac and the St. Lawrence River sit beyond it.

card.hook: Picture a narrow cobbled lane slipping away below you, with shop signs, strung lights and old facades all pointing the same way. That's Petit Champlain, and it does half your composing for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Escalier Casse-Cou (the Breakneck Stairs), on the middle section or one of its landings. Face south, looking down toward Rue du Petit-Champlain. Use a landing to step aside so you can take your time without blocking anyone.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the street falling away below you. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want more of the buildings and lights in the frame, because the narrow lane suits it well.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and keep the building edges upright so they don't lean as the street drops away.
card.best_time: Get there around 7 to 8 am, when the steps are nearly empty. The stairs and street get very busy from mid-morning. Early evening has nicer light if you don't mind people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the ivy-covered brick building at 81 Rue du Petit Champlain. One photographer calls its ivy-and-flower-basket facade charming at any time, even when the street is busy. Or try the Fresque du Petit-Champlain mural near the base of the funicular, on the Petit-Champlain side. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and stand in front of it so the mural and the area fill the background.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by at the corner of Rue du Cul-de-Sac and Rue Notre-Dame, where one guide says you can fit both Petit-Champlain and Château Frontenac in the same frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The mural area may have barriers and fencing during restoration work, so it might be partly blocked. Check the official site for closures or building works before you go.
card.challenge: Find the spot where the strung lights, the cobbles and the shop signs all line up, then take one shot with nobody in it. Early birds have the best odds.
card.good_to_know: Petit Champlain is the little cobbled lane at the foot of the cliff in Quebec City, lined with shopfronts and historic buildings. The big painted mural nearby shows scenes from the neighbourhood's history and daily life. The stairs and the street are public and need no ticket.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Escalier Casse-Cou (the Breakneck Stairs), on the middle section or one of its landings. Face south, looking down toward Rue du Petit-Champlain. Use a landing to step aside so you can take your time without blocking anyone.

card.hook: Most train stations make you rush. This one makes you stop on the lawn and wonder which fairytale king just took the 5:15. With its steep copper roofs and turrets, it looks like a small château.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place Jean-Pelletier, the grassy public lawn in front of the station, and face the front of the building. The Éclatement II fountain sits in front of you and the whole château-style façade fills the background.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole façade and the fountain in one shot. If you're close to the fountain and want it big in the foreground, try 0.5x. Use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the turrets, dormers and the clock on the roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fountain on the lower third with the turrets above it, and keep your phone level so the towers don't lean.
card.best_time: There's no single best time. Daylight is best, because you can see the stone and copper roofs clearly. The pointed roofs make a strong outline, so even a plain grey day works.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the park lawn beside the fountain, with your back to the station's front entrance. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze in more of the château, and keep the roofs and turrets over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lawn well out from the building, past the fountain, while you stand near the fountain, so the whole station fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The lawn is an open public square with no charge. The fountain isn't always running and the station has had renovation work, so the façade may look a bit different from older photos.
card.challenge: Zoom in until you can fit the roof clock and one turret in the frame, then step back and get the fountain in the foreground. Two shots, one château.
card.good_to_know: The Canadian Pacific Railway built the station in 1915, in the château style of the Loire. It looks a lot like the Château Frontenac hotel. It closed to passengers in 1976, reopened in 1985 after a major renovation, and became a Heritage Railway Station in 1992.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place Jean-Pelletier, the grassy public lawn in front of the station, and face the front of the building. The Éclatement II fountain sits in front of you and the whole château-style façade fills the background.

card.hook: Here's a fun surprise: this huge stone fortress on a clifftop isn't a museum piece, it's still a working military base. The walls look every bit as serious as that sounds, and they make a great backdrop.
card.stand_here: Stand on Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons, the elevated terrace beside the Citadelle's outer walls. The fortress itself lies about 293 m to the south-west of this point, so face south-west with the stone walls in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the walls fit with some sky above. Tap 0.5x if you want more wall in the foreground, or 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one stretch of stone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the wall along the lower third and let the sky fill the top, then keep the horizon level because the walls will make any tilt obvious.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone. It's kinder to the walls, and kinder to you too.
card.selfie_here: Try the Promenade des Gouverneurs, the elevated boardwalk under the fort walls, with the St. Lawrence River on the other side. Use the front camera, face the water and the Citadelle walls will sit behind you. You could also try 0.5x to fit more wall in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Plains of Abraham, at a point where the fort is in view, to take your photo with the walls behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Citadelle is an active military site, so the grounds are visited on guided tours and photography is restricted in some areas. Check the official site before you go, including the Changing of the Guard dates. The Promenade des Gouverneurs has many steps, so it suits you best if you're comfortable at heights and reasonably fit.
card.challenge: Get a shot with the wall along the bottom, a big slice of sky on top, and a stranger strolling along the stones for scale.
card.good_to_know: The Citadelle is a star-shaped stone fortress on Cap Diamant, the rocky headland above the St. Lawrence River. The present fortress was built between 1820 and 1850, and the Royal 22e Régiment has been based here since 1920. It sits inside Old Quebec, which became a World Heritage Site in 1985.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons, the elevated terrace beside the Citadelle's outer walls. The fortress itself lies about 293 m to the south-west of this point, so face south-west with the stone walls in front of you.

card.hook: Here's a cheat code for big-view photos: go up. The Observatoire de la Capitale sits on the 31st floor of the Marie-Guyart Building, so your phone gets a wide scene to play with instead of a street-level view.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Observatoire de la Capitale itself. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so there's no extra walk. Face the window with the clearest view and no people in the way.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the full sweep. Then go to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched shot of one landmark. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out distant details.
card.make_it_pop: Press your phone flat against the glass and cup your hand or a dark jacket around it to cut reflections.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset usually gives softer light and warmer colours. After dark, try night mode and rest your phone against a surface to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x so more of the view squeezes in behind you. Turn so the city is over your shoulder, and hold the phone close to the glass to keep reflections down.
card.rules_and_safety: Tickets must be booked online, so sort that out before you go. Check the official site for current access details.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line the horizon up with one, and add something close by in the frame for depth. Bonus points if nobody's reflection sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: The Observatoire de la Capitale is a viewing spot in Quebec City. It's on the 31st floor of the Marie-Guyart Building at 1037 Rue de la Chevrotière. The height lets you shoot a wide scene first, then zoom in on the details.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Observatoire de la Capitale itself. The phone icon on the map marks the spot, so there's no extra walk. Face the window with the clearest view and no people in the way.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where a visitor can stand with the Observatoire de la Capitale directly behind them, so I have not listed any selfie spot. The Observatoire is on the 31st floor of the Marie-Guyart Building at 1037 Rue de la Chevrotière, so a photo with it in frame would have to be taken from the street, and no source describes that. Terrasse Dufferin and Terrasse Pierre-Dugua-De-Mons are recommended for shots of Château Frontenac and the river, and the pages do not say the Observatoire is visible from them. Sources that describe the building: https://www.quebecvacances.com/en/attractions/observatoire-de-la-capitale and https://www.lonelyplanet.com/points-of-interest/observatoire-de-la-capitale/427667. Pages do say the observation windows can show reflections in photos (https://www.tripadvisor.in/Attraction_Review-g155033-d169738-Reviews-Observatoire_de_la_Capitale-Quebec_City_Quebec.html), and that tickets must be booked online (https://www.afreetourofquebec.com/post/top6quebeccity-sbestpanoramicviews). The given position, 46.80804, -71.21780, was not checked against the building's address, so please confirm it before using it on the map. A possible next step would be to search for a local photo guide that names a street-level spot showing the Marie-Guyart Building.

card.hook: Here's a photo that practically takes itself: a big fountain splashing in the foreground and a grand, very formal Parliament standing behind it like it's waiting for its portrait. Water and sculpture up front, eight floors of Second Empire drama behind.
card.stand_here: Stand in Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale, across Boulevard Honoré-Mercier from the Tourny Fountain. Face the fountain, with the Parliament façade rising behind it to the south-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the fountain with the façade behind it. If you're close and the whole front won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Save 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the statues and the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fountain on the lower third and the building in the top two thirds, then tap the building and drag the brightness down a touch so the lit fountain and the sky don't wash out.
card.best_time: Evening or after dark, when the fountain is lit. Daytime works too, but check whether event stands are in the square. One reviewer also says the building looks great at sunset or in the morning.
card.selfie_here: Stand on Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale with the Parliament behind you and face the open view toward Lower Town and the river. Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, so the building fits over your shoulder. This spot is based on a visitor tip, so test it when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Tourny Fountain facing the Parliament, so the full building fills the frame, and you pose in front of the building.
card.rules_and_safety: The fountain sits on a roundabout, so cross Boulevard Honoré-Mercier with care. In winter the Carnaval Ice Palace can block the view, so be ready to move along the pavement. Check the official site for current access to the grounds and the building.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then one close-up of a bronze statue, and see which one your friends 'like' more.
card.good_to_know: This is the home of Quebec's National Assembly, an eight-floor Second Empire building designed by Eugène-Étienne Taché. It was built between 1877 and 1886. The Assembly first met here in March 1884, two years before the work was fully finished.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Place de l'Assemblée-Nationale, across Boulevard Honoré-Mercier from the Tourny Fountain. Face the fountain, with the Parliament façade rising behind it to the south-west.

card.hook: Two buildings from very different eras share one wall here, and your phone can catch both at once. The old stone of Saint-Pierre street meets Moshe Safdie's modern design, and that mix is the whole point.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Musée de la civilisation: the phone icon on the map sits on the museum itself. Step back to the far side of the pavement if you can, and face the façade.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze more of the façade in from close range. Then step back and switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look, and use 2x for windows, stone textures or the join between old and new.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, so the walls stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to stonework than harsh midday sun. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the museum's terraces that face the St. Lawrence River, where visitors have found plenty of photo inspiration with the old stone and modern roofs around. No exact spot is given, so check on site that the museum fits behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks and flash are typically not allowed inside the museum, and photo rules can vary, so check the museum's photography policy and any signs before shooting indoors.
card.challenge: Find the exact spot where old stone meets new surface, then catch it at 2x without a single leaning line.
card.good_to_know: The museum was designed by Moshe Safdie and opened on 19 October 1988. The older Banque de Paris and Maison Estèbe buildings on Saint-Pierre street were worked into its structure. Inside, it holds more than 225,000 objects covering art, society and ethnography.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Musée de la civilisation: the phone icon on the map sits on the museum itself. Step back to the far side of the pavement if you can, and face the façade.

card.hook: Here's a fun surprise: part of this art museum used to be a prison. The Charles Baillairgé Pavilion was designed in 1867 and held prisoners until 1970, and now it sits among carved stone and sparkling glass.
card.stand_here: Start at the phone icon in the middle of the museum grounds in National Battlefields Park, just off Grande Allée. Then stroll a short way out along the park paths and turn back, so one whole pavilion fits in your picture.
card.zoom: Use 1x for the main views of each pavilion. Switch to 0.5x for the glass building and the long facades when you're close. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved reliefs and the church next door.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the glass and stone with them, keeping your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning light or a bright cloudy day keeps the reflections on the glass calm. At dusk, switch on night mode while the buildings are lit.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the forecourt in front of the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion on the Grande Allée side, with the glass lobby and the big cantilevered roof behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone offers it, so the roof makes it into the shot.
card.ask_someone: Walk along the Grande Allée sidewalk facing the museum, ask a passer-by to stand there, and pose in front of the building with the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the galleries, flash is not allowed and you need to stay at least one metre from artworks. Check the official site before you go for gallery access.
card.challenge: Catch old and new in one frame: Saint-Dominique Church and the glass of the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion side by side, with a strip of grass in front.
card.good_to_know: The Gérard-Morisset Pavilion was the first building made for the museum. It opened in June 1933, and Joseph-Émile Brunet carved the reliefs on its facade. The glass-and-steel Pierre Lassonde Pavilion arrived in 2016, designed by the Office for Metropolitan Architecture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start at the phone icon in the middle of the museum grounds in National Battlefields Park, just off Grande Allée. Then stroll a short way out along the park paths and turn back, so one whole pavilion fits in your picture.
